item.description: Donald Trump asked the Supreme Court on Sunday to let the Post Office refuse to deliver or return ballots that were already in the mail. North Carolina started mailing ballots on Friday. A federal judge blocked the Postal Service rule the same day because no state can comply with it in time. It requires every state to redesign its ballot envelopes, get the new design approved, and upload each voter's name and address to a federal portal a whistleblower says was never tested. Alabama mails on Tuesday. At least 5 more states follow next week. Trump's own lawyers told the Court that once those envelopes enter the mail stream, there is no retrieving them. He has spent a decade claiming without proof that American elections are rigged. Now he is the one changing the rules after the voting started. item.title: Nothing but an international theft organization that needs the full weight of ALL laws against.
item.description: BREAKING: Whistleblower reveals exactly what happened behind closed doors at Kennedy Center under Trump — and it’s EXPLOSIVE. Josef Palermo was the Kennedy Center's very first curator of visual arts. Soon after he accepted that position, he spent 10 months watching Donald Trump's team systematically loot, corrupt, and destroy one of America's most iconic cultural institutions. When they fired him and offered severance in exchange for his silence, he bravely said no. Now he's talking. And what he saw is worse than you even imagined. Trump appointed Richard— a former ambassador with zero arts expertise who reportedly wanted to be Secretary of State instead — to be his president of the arts institution. Palermo says that Grenell treated the Kennedy Center presidency as a consolation prize and ran the institution like a personal fiefdom and a Trump fundraising operation simultaneously. Box seats for Les Misérables went for $2 million, with a private presidential reception included. As one of Palermo's colleagues — a Republican campaign veteran — put it: "We are grafting political management principles into a nonpolitical organization." According to Palermo, the corruption was everywhere. The historic Circles Lounge was renamed the SyberJet Lounge — after an aircraft company whose CEO had been convicted of defrauding investors and received a Trump pardon. The African Room, filled with priceless artifacts representing African cultural heritage, was renamed "A Tribute to America's Intelligence Community" and handed to a donor the Wall Street Journal described as someone who allegedly lied about being in the CIA. Priceless handmade African textiles, a wooden sculpture donated by Ghana to mourn President Kennedy's assassination, and doors carved from 700-year-old wood depicting Yoruban village scenes were taken down. Palermo was never told where they went. At an October 7th anniversary commemoration in the Israeli Lounge — an event honoring victims of a pogrom — Grenell used the occasion to shake down the Jewish attendees for donations, warning that the lounge would be "given away" to a new sponsor if they didn't write checks. "It certainly would be a shame if we lost this room," he said. Palermo was mortified. One of Grenell's lieutenants texted Palermo asking if the Center could "do something" with an artist whose work Grenell personally owned — a move that would have increased the artwork's auction value and directly benefited Grenell. Palermo ignored the request. Meanwhile, Grenell instituted a return-to-office mandate that applied to everyone except himself. While staffers' meeting requests went unanswered, Grenell was posting Instagram photos from a yacht off the coast of Croatia. The Kennedy Center now denies this happened, despite the existence of the Instagram posts. Then came the order that stopped Palermo cold. Grenell told him to "get rid of everything" in the permanent collection — including the eight-foot, 3,000-pound brass bust of President Kennedy that has stood in the Grand Foyer since the center opened. If donors wouldn't pay for removal, Grenell said, they could auction the works off or give them away. When Palermo reported this to another senior leader, the man's eyes went wide. He told Palermo to do nothing and said his office would handle it. The roof was leaking. The willow trees outside were rotting. The fundraising operation couldn't pay its postage invoices. But the high-priority renovation? Gold gilding on the chandelier of the presidential box in the Opera House. Grenell's grand vision for America's 250th birthday celebration at the nation's premier cultural center? An America's Got Talent-style talent show. We’re not kidding. Palermo refused the gag order. He is now cooperating with Senator Sheldon Whitehouse's investigation and has been in contact with Representative Joyce Beatty's legal team, which is suing to stop the renaming of the center. "There must be a firewall put in place by Congress to prevent this kind of hostile political takeover of the Kennedy Center from ever happening again," he wrote. The Kennedy Center was built as a living memorial to President John F. Kennedy — a gift to the American people and a symbol of this nation's commitment to art, culture, and the best of what humanity can create. Trump renamed it after himself, tried to sell its lounges to Kazakhstan, ordered its permanent collection disposed of, and ran it into the ground in less than a year. The bust of President Kennedy still stands in the Grand Foyer. For now. Please like and share this post if you believe America's cultural institutions belong to the American people — not to Trump's donors, Trump's pardoned felons, and Trump's Instagram feed. Check out the NPR article on this.

item.title: Wonderful workaround!
item.description: A newborn died in Nashville overnight on September 10, 2001. His family, in the worst hours of their lives, decided to donate his organs. Only the liver could be used. Early the next morning a match came back: a 6-month-old girl in Houston named Kareena, dying of liver failure. A charter plane was booked and the recovery surgery at Vanderbilt Children's Hospital was nearly finished. Then the country closed. Jill Grandas ran Tennessee Donor Services. Her phone rang, and it was her own staff member standing in the operating room. "What are we going to do? No planes are allowed to leave the ground." There was a liver in a cooler with hours left on it, a baby in Texas who did not have longer, and not one civilian aircraft in America was permitted to move. So Grandas reached for the phone book. "Believe it or not, 20 years ago in the blue pages, there was a listing for the tower," she said. Somebody at Nashville International picked up, handed her to a supervisor, and the supervisor's calls reached Senator Bill Frist, a transplant surgeon before he was a politician, who did not need the situation explained to him. The Tennessee Air National Guard was cleared to fly. They started up a C-130 Hercules, an aircraft built to carry a tank, and put 10 ounces in it. "We usually take some pretty interesting things in the back of a C-130," co-pilot John Howard said. "And that was probably the lightest payload, next to being empty, that I've ever flown in my life." Nobody spoke for the first half of the flight. The sky was empty and patrolled by fighters, and the crew understood what could happen to an aircraft that appeared where it should not be. They landed in Houston and handed the cooler over without shutting down the engines. Dr. John Goss was waiting at Texas Children's Hospital. The transplant went smoothly. Kareena is 25 now. "All these people who didn't know this little baby, who had no connection with this child, worked together on a day that really tested our nation," she said. This week, 25 years later, she finally met Jill Grandas in person.

item.title: An Atlas a day!
item.description:
I don’t have any new Atlas for you, so here are some then and now photos. I’ve shared this before, but this was his adoption profile photo. Somebody threw this thing in a dumpster. I mean, he was an actual terrorist as a baby, and there were times I’d give the empty threat of putting him back in the trash. But I truly can’t imagine doing this to any creature.
Same dumb dumb baby, three years later. It’s been the most loaded and taxing three years of my life. I would not be here if not for this dog.
Yep, one photo to sum up his puppyhood.
Always teefs. Always upside down.
Is this blep or mlem?
Blep or mlem?
I was sad on my birthday, because I’m always sad on my birthday. I can’t bring myself to celebrate, and if I try, it never seems to work out. And it’s hard to want to celebrate the day when it’s also the day I lost my soul dog, my world at the time, my existential guide dog. I was sad, but also kind of numb. I was surprisingly not as heavy with grief as I thought I’d be. But you know, grief can be a sneaky little asshole, and it waits a few days to clothesline the wind out of you when you suspect it less. Today was a hard day. Grief annihilated me from the inside out, like a rototiller that somehow had the power to eviscerate my body, heart, and soul all at once, and to varying degrees of destruction. All the giant life problems I put aside so I could focus on healing came thundering back down on me like the fists of titans. And I mostly got walloped in the guts with grief like hot lead. I miss my dog. I miss him so much. I miss my cat. I miss their friendship. I miss the three of us in a pile on the couch. Atlas has grown to be my world, and I’m so grateful he came into my life, even under the most difficult circumstances. I love him with everything that I have and everything that I am. But I’ll always miss Seymour from the deepest part of my being. So, I was sad today. And I just let myself be sad. I didn’t fight it. I didn’t try to force it into something productive. I just cried a lot. And Atlas gently curled himself up onto my still broken body, and he just let me cry. I’m grateful to be healing. I’m grateful to have time to rest. I’m just struggling with these physical limitations on top of everything. I’m struggling with navigating new and different pain. I’m just struggling inside of my body and my brain. My shoulder has really been bothering since it opened up. It’s still clean and healthy, but I just have this gaping hole in my shoulder and it’s hard to find a position that feels comfortable. My insides still feel like they’re on fire. I’m just so very tired. And today, well today was the day grief chose to rear its head like an angry bull. My grief feels as hot as my insides. It’s days like these, where dare I say with trepidation and vulnerability, that I just wish I had the closeness and connection with another human that afforded me the opportunity to be held, and really seen, and just loved in the midst of this vulnerability. A human to help me change this bandage so I don’t have to contort myself in ridiculous ways to do it myself. Today is just tough. My body hurts. My heart hurts. My brain hurts. But I love my sweet boy, as much as I miss my old boy. And at least I’ve got that. Much love.

And, in so doing, they bound themselves to everything that came after. Who cares any more what particular knot they used in the binding?” -A.R. Moxon

But they are amusing themselves, for it is their adversary who is obliged to use words responsibly, since he believes in words. The anti-Semites have the right to play. They even like to play with discourse for, by giving ridiculous reasons, they discredit the seriousness of their interlocutors. They delight in acting in bad faith, since they seek not to persuade by sound argument but to intimidate and disconcert.
